lead: The first law of thermodynamics says energy is conserved. For a closed system, the heat added minus the work done equals the change in the energy stored inside; over a complete cycle, net heat equals net work. This one balance finds an unknown heat, work or energy change in any process, gives the area inside a p-V loop a meaning, and rules out any machine that claims to create energy.
prereq: You need: the closed system, state, path and cycle, and the sign convention for work and heat (see Work and heat: definitions and sign convention, and Displacement work and other work modes).

blocks.text: A system stores energy in three forms: kinetic energy KE = mV²/2 of the system moving as a whole at velocity V (m/s); potential energy PE = mgz of its height z (m) above a datum, with g = 9.81 m/s²; and internal energy U, the energy of the molecules themselves. The total stored energy is E = U + KE + PE, in kJ.

Energy crosses the boundary of a closed system in only two ways: as heat Q, driven by a temperature difference, and as work W (a moving piston, a turning shaft, an electric current). Heat and work are energy in transit, not stored energy.
Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = E₂ − E₁ = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE
blocks.where: Q₁₂ is the heat added to the system from state 1 to state 2 (kJ); W₁₂ is the work done by the system (kJ); ΔU, ΔKE and ΔPE are the changes in internal, kinetic and potential energy (kJ).

blocks.text: Most exam systems do not move as a whole, so ΔKE = ΔPE = 0 and the law takes its usual form below. Keep the full form for a falling or moving system.

blocks.where: the process form for a stationary closed system; all terms in kJ.

blocks.text: Signs: heat added to the system and work done by the system are positive; heat rejected and work done on the system are negative. Chemistry books count W as work done on the system and write Q + W = ΔU; both are correct if used consistently, but this book uses Q − W = ΔU throughout.

blocks.where: δQ and δW are small heat and work transfers in an infinitesimal step, written with δ because they depend on the path; dU is the small change of the property U.

blocks.text: Over a complete cycle the system returns to state 1, so ΔU = 0 and the balance becomes ∮δQ = ∮δW, where ∮ means the sum around the whole cycle: net heat in equals net work out. A control mass means the same as a closed system.

sections.h3: Heat and work follow the path; U does not

blocks.text: U depends only on the state, so ΔU between two states is fixed; Q and W depend on the route.

Both paths give ΔU = 50 kJ. You can say “the internal energy of state 2”, never “the heat of state 2”. An isolated system has Q = W = 0, so its energy stays constant, and a cycle with net work but no net heat is the impossible perpetual motion machine of the first kind.

sections.h3: Moving boundary work is the area under the process curve

blocks.text: When a piston moves slowly enough for the gas to stay in equilibrium (a quasi-static process), the work done by the gas is the area under its path on a p-V diagram:

blocks.where: p is the absolute pressure of the gas (kPa) and dV the small volume change (m³); the integral runs along the actual path. W comes out in kJ when p is in kPa and V in m³. At constant pressure it is simply p(V₂ − V₁).

blocks.text: Expansion gives W > 0, compression W < 0. Two paths between the same end states have different areas under their curves, which is why W depends on the path. For a cycle the net work is the area enclosed by the loop, positive when it runs clockwise, and it equals the net heat.

∫p dV needs a quasi-static path. A gas rushing into a vacuum when a membrane bursts (free expansion) grows in volume but pushes on nothing, so W = 0. Slow, resisted expansion is the ideal of a reversible process; a sudden one is irreversible (see Reversible and irreversible processes).

figure.caption: Left: in process 1 → 2 the gas takes in 80 kJ of heat and does 30 kJ of work, so 50 kJ stays as internal energy. Right: the return path 2 → 1 rejects 70 kJ while 20 kJ of work is done on the gas; the loop encloses the net work, 10 kJ, which equals the net heat.

spec.aria: Left: a piston-cylinder with a dashed boundary; 80 kJ of heat enters, 30 kJ of work leaves through the piston rod, and the gas gains 50 kJ of internal energy. Right: a p-V loop from state 1 to state 2 along an upper expansion path and back along a lower dashed path; the shaded loop is labelled 10 kJ.

examples.question: A gas in a piston-cylinder device receives 80 kJ of heat and does 30 kJ of work as it goes from state 1 to state 2. (a) Find the change in internal energy. (b) The gas is then brought back to state 1 along a path in which 20 kJ of work is done on the gas. Find the heat transfer for the return path. (c) Verify the cycle form of the first law.
steps: Path 1 → 2: U₂ − U₁ = Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = 80 − 30 = +50 kJ.
For the return path 2 → 1 the internal-energy change reverses: U₁ − U₂ = −50 kJ.
Work is done on the gas, so W₂₁ = −20 kJ by the sign convention.
Rearrange: Q₂₁ = ΔU + W₂₁ = −50 + (−20) = −70 kJ. The gas rejects 70 kJ of heat.
Net heat over the cycle: Q<sub>net</sub> = 80 − 70 = 10 kJ. Net work: W<sub>net</sub> = 30 − 20 = 10 kJ.
Q<sub>net</sub> = W<sub>net</sub> = 10 kJ, so ∮δQ = ∮δW is satisfied, and the loop of Figure 2.1.1 encloses 10 kJ.
examples.answer: ΔU = +50 kJ for 1 → 2; the return path rejects 70 kJ of heat; over the cycle Q<sub>net</sub> = W<sub>net</sub> = 10 kJ.

examples.question: Gas in a cylinder at a constant 200 kPa expands from 0.05 m³ to 0.15 m³ while 50 kJ of heat is added. Find the boundary work and the change in internal energy.
steps: Constant pressure: W = p(V₂ − V₁) = 200 × (0.15 − 0.05) = 20 kJ (kPa × m³ = kJ), positive, so done by the gas.
First law: ΔU = Q − W = 50 − 20 = 30 kJ.
examples.answer: W = 20 kJ done by the gas and ΔU = +30 kJ; of the 50 kJ added, 30 kJ stays in the gas and 20 kJ leaves as work.

traps: Calling Q or W a property: “the heat of state 2” is wrong; only U (and E) is stored and fixed by the state.
Sign slip when work is done on the system: W = −20 kJ, not +20 kJ. Taking +20 in Q = ΔU + W gives −50 + 20 = −30 kJ instead of the correct −70 kJ.
Using ∫p dV for a free expansion into a vacuum. The volume changes but the gas pushes on nothing, so W = 0.
Using Q − W = ΔU for a turbine, nozzle or any open system. Mass carries energy in and out there; use the steady flow energy equation.

quiz.q: State the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system undergoing a process.
quiz.a: Heat added minus work done by the system equals the change in its stored energy: Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = E₂ − E₁, which is U₂ − U₁ for a system at rest.

quiz.q: Why is U called a property but Q is not?
quiz.a: U is fixed by the state, so ΔU between two states is the same along every path. Q is energy in transit and changes with the path, so it belongs to the process, not the state.

quiz.q: A gas absorbs 120 kJ of heat and its internal energy falls by 40 kJ. Find the work done, with its sign.
quiz.a: Q − W = ΔU, so W = Q − ΔU = 120 − (−40) = 160 kJ. Positive, so 160 kJ of work is done by the gas.

quiz.q: A 2 kg stone falls 10 m inside a closed, insulated box and comes to rest at the bottom. What happens to its 196 J of potential energy?
quiz.a: Q = 0 and W = 0 for the box, so ΔE = 0: ΔU + ΔPE = 0. PE falls by mgz = 2 × 9.81 × 10 = 196.2 J, so U of the box contents rises by 196.2 J; the stone and floor warm slightly.

quiz.q: A student writes Q + W = ΔU but takes W as positive when done by the system. Show with the cycle form why this mix fails.
quiz.a: Around a cycle ΔU = 0, so the student gets Q<sub>net</sub> = −W<sub>net</sub>: an engine that delivers work would need negative net heat, which contradicts ∮δQ = ∮δW. Q + W = ΔU is right only when W means work done on the system; with W done by the system the law is Q − W = ΔU.

beyond: Plant energy audits apply the first-law balance to every stream of a boiler or chiller to find where energy leaves unused. Computational fluid dynamics solves conservation equations for mass, momentum and energy in every small cell of a flow, which grow out of the same balance. Battery engineers use it to size cooling: when a pack’s stored energy is steady, its coolant must carry away the electrical energy lost inside it. Search “control mass energy balance” and “p-V diagram cycle work”.
